1.text: ATHLETIC SPORTS. — The Chukchee are fond of all kinds of sports, and

2.text: indulge in them whenever opportunity is offered. Many of their games are

3.text: connected with religious ceremonials, as will be described later.

4.text: Among the Reindeer Chukchee the chief sport is reindeer-racing. Once

5.text: a year almost every camp arranges a race. These races are held in circuits,

6.text: so that the whole neighborhood can visit all in their vicinity. The principal

7.text: man of the camp, who figures as the host of the race (ireˊlɪn), has to supply

8.text: the prize, which varies from a couple of leaves of tobacco to a beaver-skin

9.text: or a pack-sledge reindeer. The prize is tied to a tree-branch, which is stuck

10.text: into the snow. For this reason it is called “the thing stuck in” (rɪˊpyo). The

11.text: larger the prize, the greater will be the concourse of people at the race, and

12.text: the longer the stretch to be covered by the contestants, sometimes ten miles

14.text: There are no particular rules about starting the race. The participants

15.text: gather in front of the prize in an irregular group. The host gives the signal,

16.text: and all start off. While some keep to the road, others strike off through the

17.text: deep snow, trying to intercept the leaders. The race is to a distant point

18.text: and back again. Until the contestants are on the return stretch they spare

19.text: their animals. The race begins in earnest on the way back, and becomes

20.text: very exciting as they near the prize.

21.text: The onlookers are very enthusiastic, and meet the racers with encouraging

22.text: cries or hootings. The winner snatches the prize, and the race is over. Often

23.text: one or two minor prizes are also put up by other people of the camp. These

24.text: are taken by the next comers in order. Sometimes there is also a small stake

25.text: for the last comer, partly in derision, partly (according to a native saying)

26.text: “to console him for his disgrace.” The host takes part in the race, but it is

27.text: regarded as discourteous if he seriously tries to beat his guests out of the

28.text: prize. If he comes in first, he will not touch the prize; or, if there is more

29.text: than one prize, he will take the smallest, leaving the others for his guests.

30.text: The Chukchee are passionately fond of reindeer-racing. In the spring,

31.text: which is the usual season for the sport, some of the young people undertake

32.text: long journeys to try their reindeer against a possible rival. Doubtful races

33.text: often lead to quarrels, and even to feuds. I had a chance to observe one of

34.text: these in 1896 in the East Anui camps on the Wolverene River. Two rivals

35.text: of several years standing met in a race. When one had almost reached the

36.text: goal, one of his reindeer suddenly stumbled and fell, thus allowing the other
